title: Empathy and compassion
hookLine: feeling another's pain can overwhelm; compassion adds warmth and the wish to help (Singer and Klimecki)

cards: A friend calls, crying. Within a minute, the one listening can find a tight chest, a thick throat, tears close behind. It can look like love at its fullest.
And sometimes, an hour later, that same listener is wrung out, a little shaky, and dreading the next call. Is that what caring has to cost? A new stretch of the path starts here: compassion.
It opens with a distinction that sounds like hair-splitting until it's been lived. Feeling with someone, and feeling for them, may not be the same thing at all.

teach.b: First, empathy. In the work of neuroscientist Tania Singer and psychologist Olga Klimecki, empathy means sharing another person's feeling: their pain becomes, in a small way, your pain.
That's a real and good capacity; it's how we know someone is hurting at all.
Second, the trouble with empathy alone. When people were trained only to feel along with others' suffering, Singer and Klimecki reported, their own negative feelings went up.
Feeling with someone, over and over, with nowhere to go, can tip into what they called empathic distress. Drowning alongside. Third, compassion.

teach.h: COMPASSION: WARMTH AND A WISH TO HELP.
teach.b: They describe it as something added on top: warmth toward the person, concern for them, and a wish to help. It still sees the pain, but it doesn't merge with it.
People trained in compassion reported more positive feeling, even while looking at others' suffering, and their brain scans showed different networks at work.

Fourth, an old word, one this path first met on day three hundred thirteen. Buddhist teaching names compassion as one of four boundless qualities, alongside loving-kindness, sympathetic joy and equanimity.
The Pali and Sanskrit word is karuna, which teachers in that tradition describe as the wish that beings be free from suffering. A wish, notice. Not a flood.
The lifeguard who jumps in and panics with the swimmer helps no one. The one who stays steady, warm and moving toward them can pull them out.

how: In Buddhist practice, compassion (karuna) is cultivated as one of four boundless qualities, often by holding someone in mind and wishing them free from suffering; contemplative researchers have taught a similar shift from sharing pain to warm concern.

o: feeling with someone vs. warmth and a wish to help
being polite to people you don't really like
two names for one and the same feeling of pity

games.q: feeling with and feeling for: tap the pairs.
p: warmth and a wish to help
the wish that beings be free from suffering

s: in the research, training only in empathy raised people's own negative feelings
feeling with others' pain, again and again, tipped toward distress.
compassion means refusing to look at someone's pain
compassion still sees the pain; it adds warmth and the wish to help instead of merging with it.

games.q: a friend is sobbing on the phone and you feel yourself going under with them. what does compassion training suggest?
o: stay, and turn the shared pain into warmth and a wish to help.
feel it as hard as you can to prove you care.
games.why: the researchers described compassion as warmth and concern added on top of seeing the pain, which kept people steadier.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is struggling right now, and let yourself feel a little of what they feel for a breath or two, without forcing it.
Then gently change the angle: turn toward them with warmth, the way you might put a hand on a shoulder, and hold one simple wish for them, may this ease.

wordCard.voice: Empathy and compassion. Empathy feels with someone; compassion adds warmth and the wish to help, so care doesn't turn into drowning. Today's word.

orig.note: karuna: compassion in Pali and Sanskrit, one of the four boundless qualities in Buddhist teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: warmth, not drowning. Care can see the pain without going under with it. Until tomorrow.
